footer.coverage: Two sources, kept apart on purpose. Vacancy counts are live openings registered at the Czech Labour Office (Úřad práce ČR). They are real postings, though the register leans toward service, trades and operational roles, so higher-skill and senior corporate counts read low. Every salary figure comes instead from the official ISPV earnings survey and its regional RSCP cut: what people are actually paid, not what a posting advertises. Figures are workplace-based, so a region reflects what employers there pay rather than what residents earn. Where the survey has no figure, we leave it out rather than estimate it.

calibration.title: How accurate are we?
calibration.blurb: Whether a fit score actually predicts the recruiter's decision. Each dot is a score band. Where it sits versus the dashed line is how calibrated we are.
calibration.measuresPipeline: Measures the pipeline match score against whether the candidate advanced past screening or was rejected there. That score is the number screening auto-decisions act on.
calibration.measuresAnalysis: Measures the saved CV-analysis score against recruiter advance/pass dispositions on analyses. This score never gates pipeline decisions.
calibration.uncalibratedBody: Calibration needs at least {min} decided candidates (advanced or passed). So far: {n}.
calibration.exclusionPipeline: a candidate counts once they're decided at screening: advanced (reached interview, offer, or hired) or rejected there. Still-pending, declined, role-closed, withdrawn, and unscored candidates are excluded until they're decided.
calibration.exclusionAnalysis: an analysis counts once you record a disposition: advance or pass. Held and undecided analyses are excluded.
calibration.driftBlurb: Brier per quarter (lower is better). A recent slip can hide inside a good all-time score.
calibration.bandsBlurb: Each band lists the candidates behind that dot. Open one to see who scored there.
calibration.recLower: Candidates scoring {lo}–{hi} advanced past screening {pct}% of the time (n={n}). Your auto-reject floor is {current}. Consider lowering it to {suggested}.
calibration.recRaise: Candidates scoring {lo}–{hi} advanced past screening only {pct}% of the time (n={n}). Your auto-reject floor is {current}. Consider raising it to {suggested}.
calibration.recBasis: Based on {total} decided candidates. This is only a suggestion. Nothing changes until you apply it.
calibration.recApplied: Auto-reject floor set to {suggested} (was {previous}). Reversible from Decision rules.
calibration.recFamilyInfo: This suggestion is scoped to the selected role family, but the auto-reject floor is a single, global setting. Switch to all roles to apply it.
calibration.historyBlurb: Every applied change to the screening floor: sealed, tamper-evident, and measured.
calibration.historyBasis: Band {lo}–{hi} advanced {pct}% of the time (n={n}) when applied.
calibration.effectTooFew: Too few decisions in band {lo}–{hi} since the change to measure. At least {min} are needed.
calibration.effectAfterOnly: Since then, {pct}% of band {lo}–{hi} candidates advanced (n={n}). No earlier in-band decisions to compare against.
calibration.effectDelta: Band {lo}–{hi} advance rate: {beforePct}% before → {afterPct}% after the change (n={n} since).
calibration.recAppliedFamily: {family} floor set to {suggested} (was {previous}). Reversible by re-applying.
calibration.familyFloorsBlurb: Families with their own auto-reject floor (global floor: {global}). Select one to review or adjust it.
calibration.measuresHoldout: Measures the pipeline match score against candidates the screening wave spared from auto-rejection. Their outcome was not produced by the score, so this is the one arm the calibration can be falsified against.
calibration.exclusionHoldout: a spared candidate counts once a decision is reached: advanced past screening, or rejected later by a person. Candidates the floor never touched, and those still pending, are excluded.
calibration.leakageScoreCausedNote: The rejection is produced by the score itself: automatic screening rejects on the match score, so this curve largely validates the score against its own decisions. The Brier score is biased optimistic by an amount nothing here estimates.
calibration.leakageScoreCausedCeiling: Only the holdout arm breaks this coupling. Until it has accrued enough outcomes, read this curve as internal consistency, not accuracy.
calibration.leakageReviewerSawNote: The outcome is a human advance/pass decision, so the score did not mechanically produce it. But the recruiter saw the score while deciding, so the two are correlated by anchoring rather than independent.
calibration.leakageReviewerSawCeiling: Not a score-blind trial: the decision was informed by the very number being validated.
calibration.leakageCleanArmNote: These candidates scored below the auto-reject floor and were spared anyway, so the score did not mechanically produce their outcome. This is the arm the calibration can actually be falsified against.
calibration.leakageCleanArmCeiling: The reviewer still saw the score, so this is not fully score-blind; and the arm covers only the range below the floor, so it can tell you whether your rejections were right, not whether the whole curve is.
calibration.accrualTitle: When this arm can be judged
calibration.accrualBody: About {remaining} more decided candidates ({n} of {min} so far). Until then this stays a horizon, not a curve.
calibration.accrualHoldout: The holdout only fills while auto-rejection is running: a sampled share of the candidates it would reject is spared and tracked here.
calibration.skillHint: 0 % = no better than always predicting this cohort’s base rate ({pct} % advanced, Brier {base}). Below zero is worse than that.
calibration.recLeakageCaveat: This suggestion reads the band advance rates that the floor you are about to move helped produce, so it is partly circular. Check it against the clean arm once that arm can be judged.
calibration.recAbsentBody: Neither score band next to your auto-reject floor of {current} carries enough decided candidates, at a clearly high or low advance rate, to defend a move. That is an absence of evidence, not an endorsement of the current floor.
calibration.recAbsentNoFloor: No auto-reject floor is in force, so there is nothing to move. Set one in Decision rules if screening should act on this score.
calibration.recAbsentFamily: Measured within {family} only. The all-roles view may still hold enough to say something.
calibration.familyFloorsNone: No role family carries its own floor, so every family is screened at the global {global}.
calibration.measuresPipelineHired: Measures the pipeline match score against whether the candidate was actually hired. Reaching the hire takes interviews, an offer and an acceptance, so this is a much harder question than advancing past screening, and a much slower one to answer.
calibration.measuresHoldoutHired: Measures the pipeline match score against whether candidates the screening wave spared from auto-rejection were actually hired. Nothing automatic produced that outcome, so this is the strictest arm the calibration offers.
calibration.exclusionPipelineHired: a candidate counts once they are hired or rejected. Everyone still in the process is excluded, because they may yet be hired. Candidates who declined, whose role closed, who withdrew, or who have no score are excluded as well: none of that is a verdict on the candidate.
calibration.exclusionHoldoutHired: a spared candidate counts once they are hired or rejected. Candidates the floor never touched, and everyone still in the process, are excluded.
calibration.outcomeAnalysisUnavailable: This arm records a recruiter decision on an analysis, not a pipeline stage, so it cannot say who was hired. Switch to the pipeline match score for that.
calibration.outcomeHiredScopeNote: The score-band drilldown and the threshold suggestion are both derived from advancing past screening, so they stay on that setting. Switch back to see them.
calibration.skillHintHired: 0 % = no better than always predicting this cohort’s base rate ({pct} % hired, Brier {base}). Below zero is worse than that.
calibration.uncalibratedBodyHired: Calibration needs at least {min} candidates who were hired or rejected. So far: {n}.
calibration.leakageScoreCausedHiredNote: Reaching the hire takes interviews, an offer and an acceptance, none of which this score decides, so the successes here were not produced by the score. The rejections partly were: automatic screening rejects on the match score, and each of those counts here as not hired. This axis is less circular than the screening one, not clean.
calibration.leakageScoreCausedHiredCeiling: Everyone still in the process is excluded until they are hired or rejected, so this axis fills slowly and leans on whoever left early. It also says nothing about how a hire then performed.

decisionRecords.keylessExplain: The seal is a public SHA-256 with no secret, so the chain catches accidental corruption, a deleted row and a careless edit. But anyone who can write to the database can recompute every link and forge it undetected. Set KP_DECISION_HMAC_KEY to seal new records under a key the database writer does not hold.
decisionRecords.keylessCeiling: Turning the key on later cannot re-seal what is already here: {keyless, plural, one {this # record stays} other {these # records stay}} keyless for good. The key protects every record sealed after it, and from the first keyed record on, an edit to an earlier one breaks the chain at that point.

hashChain.name: Tamper-evident hash chain
hashChain.proves: Every observed step is chained server-side as it happens, so a session cannot be quietly rewritten afterwards. A link that fails to recompute, or a client clock that contradicts when the server received the event, marks the whole trace untrustworthy rather than merely odd.

promptCapture.name: Prompt capture
promptCapture.proves: The assistant and stakeholder exchanges the candidate wrote are part of the record. Model use is graded on how they drove it (decomposition, iteration, asking it to verify itself), never on volume, and never as a penalty.

canaries.name: Planted canaries
canaries.proves: The starter repo carries deliberate flaws, each with one checkable truth. Every one comes back addressed, flagged, propagated or unverifiable. A planted flaw that survived into the submission is generated output that was shipped unread.

perturbation.name: Mid-flight perturbation
perturbation.proves: A requirement moves while the work is open, server-timestamped. Everything after that moment is adaptation to a brief no prepared answer anticipated; absorbing it is judgment you can watch happen.

watermark.name: Session watermark
watermark.proves: Each session's work carries its own reference. Another session's reference turning up inside this one is decisive evidence a solution circulated between candidates. A narrow control, deliberately: on its own, a missing marker is a note for the reviewer, never a verdict.

meta.description: How KandiDate processes candidate and workspace data: consent, retention, erasure, AI transparency, subprocessors and billing.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: KandiDate is hiring software. It reads CVs, runs interviews and records hiring decisions, so this policy is written around the data those features actually touch. It describes shipped behavior, and where a control is configurable, it says so.

roles.title: Who is responsible for your data
roles.controller: For candidate data (CVs, interview transcripts, scorecards and decision records), the company running the hiring workspace is the data controller. It decides why and how candidates are assessed.
roles.processor: The KandiDate vendor acts as a processor for that data: it processes candidate data only to provide the product to the controller, under the controller's configuration and instructions.
roles.account: For the customer's own workspace account and billing data, the KandiDate vendor is the controller.

data.title: What the product processes
data.intro: The product processes only what the hiring flow needs:
items: CV documents and the text extracted from them
Voice interview audio, transcripts and structured scorecards
Job-fit scores, evidence and salary estimates derived from the CV
Decision records: who was advanced, rejected or offered, when, and why
Contact details used to reach a candidate about their application
Workspace account, plan and usage data for the customer

consent.title: Consent and retention
consent.gate: Consent is captured before any AI reads a candidate's data, and candidate pages state that an AI is involved before it happens, not after.
consent.retention: Recruitment consent expires. In this deployment the retention window is up to {months} months from the moment consent is given. The window is configurable per deployment, and the figure shown here is derived from the live configuration rather than typed by hand, so it cannot drift from what is enforced.
consent.expiry: When consent expires, the record is anonymized: the name is reduced to a non-identifying handle, contact details, the CV text and verbatim quotes are removed, and non-identifying recruitment signals (skills, scores, seniority, salary band) are retained so the controller can keep lawful hiring statistics.
consent.readGate: Expiry also takes effect immediately at read time: the product withholds CV text and transcripts even before the periodic anonymization sweep has run, and suppresses any further outreach to that candidate.

rights.title: Your rights as a candidate
rights.intro: Every candidate receives a personal token link. It requires no account, and it opens a page where you can:
items: See the data held about you, including the decisions recorded about your application
Ask for human review of any decision an AI was involved in
rights.erasure: Erasure runs as a single transaction across your profile, interview transcripts, scorecards and the message outbox: it completes in full or not at all.
rights.carveout: One category is exempt from erasure: sealed decision records. They are retained under Article 17(3)(b) and (e) GDPR, because a regulated hiring decision must remain auditable and defensible after the fact. Once you are erased, they refer to you only by a masked, non-identifying reference.

voice.title: Voice interviews
voice.body: A voice interview is recorded and transcribed only after you explicitly consent on the interview page. That consent is enforced on the server: without it the interview session is never created and no transcript is stored. You can decline, and your application continues without a voice interview.

ai.title: AI transparency
ai.oversight: Under the EU AI Act, screening, scoring, ranking and interviewing candidates is a high-risk use. Every candidate-facing page shows an AI disclosure before an AI reads your data, as Article 50 requires.
ai.sealed: No candidate is advanced, rejected or offered by the machine alone. Every adverse decision requires a human, and every decision, human or automated, is sealed into a tamper-evident audit record stating who made it and why.

subprocessors.title: Subprocessors
subprocessors.body: The product routes to the providers each customer configures, so the set it can engage is: {list}. None of them is mandatory: a self-hosted, offline installation engages no external processor at all. Candidate data is never sold or shared, and is never used to train models.
subprocessors.trustLink: The maintained list, together with the product's article-by-article EU AI Act posture, is published on the trust page.

billing.title: Billing data
billing.body: Paid plans are sold through Polar, acting as merchant of record. Polar processes payment details and issues invoices; card data never reaches KandiDate. The product stores only the subscription state needed to meter usage.

security.title: Security
items: Provider API keys are stored write-only and encrypted at rest; they never round-trip to a browser
Each workspace's data is isolated per tenant
Decision records are sealed into a tamper-evident hash chain with key rotation
An offline mode blocks all model egress, for air-gapped and in-VPC installs

about.title: Six mechanisms, shown running
about.intro: Hiring software asks you to trust a number. These are the six places this product produces one: how a role gets written, how a person gets scored, who gets filtered and by what, how different kinds of candidate are kept from being flattened into one rule, what a work sample can still prove, and where a human has to decide. Every threshold named below is a constant in the running code.
about.tourTitle: Walk the pipeline live, across the real tabs

jd.title: Three passes, and nothing invented
jd.lede: You tick what should be built, and an unticked step never spawns a process. One pass reads your need against the real codebase and reports where they disagree; a second turns it into requirements that must trace back to something actually stated; a third prices the band from the open web. The last two run side by side. The document itself is then assembled in code rather than written by the model.

scoring.title: Three answers, not two
scoring.lede: A required skill scores between zero and one against the profile, and where it lands decides how it gets reported. Above 0.5 it counts as matched, carried with its strength so a 0.55 is never shown as a 1.0. Below 0.5 but above zero it is unproven, and it says why: the evidence was adjacent, or it was weakly sourced, or both. Only an exact zero is called missing. A product with two buckets has to call a weak signal either a match or a gap, and both of those are wrong.

screening.title: Cheap filters first, expensive judgement last
screening.lede: Screening is ordered by cost. Hard gates run on everyone, a deterministic scorer runs on whoever survives, and the model is asked to reason only about the shortlist that reaches the top. Nothing that costs money runs on a candidate who was already ruled out.

archetypes.title: The same three slots, weighted differently
archetypes.lede: A student and a fifteen-year veteran cannot be ranked by one rule without one of them losing unfairly. So a candidate is routed to an archetype, and the archetype changes what the three scoring dimensions mean: for early-career profiles, Career becomes Potential and Personal becomes Fit. Two of the three archetypes are fairness-protected and can never be auto-rejected.

assignments.title: A work sample that survives being delegated
assignments.lede: Anyone can hand a take-home to a model. So the assignment is built to be informative even then: it carries deliberate under-specification, traps that punish confident guessing, and a mid-flight change that arrives after the work has started. What is graded is the reasoning the candidate shows, not whether the answer compiles.

gates.title: The machine ranks, a person decides
gates.lede: Every action that reaches a candidate passes a person first. The system's job is to arrive at that moment with the evidence assembled and the reasoning written down: what was scored, on what basis, and what it was not confident about. The decision a person then makes is recorded as theirs.

archetypes.declaration: If the candidate declared an archetype themselves, that declaration wins and is trusted at 0.9. A contradicting signal never overrides it. It lowers the confidence to 0.65 and appends a reason, which the soft-signal panel then republishes for a human to look at.
archetypes.fallback: When nothing fires at all the result is <k>bau</k> at 0.4. That number sits below the 0.55 review threshold on purpose, so a routing decision made with no evidence always shows up as one that needs checking rather than passing quietly as a result.

gates.noteRejection: The rejection row is the one that matters. The pass computes it, clears it through the fairness gate, and then refuses to apply it, queueing it for a person instead. A rejection is the one irreversible, candidate-visible adverse action in the product, so nothing applies one on its own.
gates.noteAutonomous: Advances, holds, alerts, scoring and drafting stay autonomous, and naming that plainly is what makes the rest of the claim worth anything.
gates.noteHired: Hired is not on this road at all. A manual move to Hired returns 422, because that stage is set when the candidate accepts an offer and by nothing else.
